claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Dislocations pile up at internal boundaries in the untreated alloy.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations.
The local stress concentrations promote microcracking and brittle failure during straining.
The untreated alloy has high strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
The proposed intervention is controlled deformation followed by optimized annealing.
The thermomechanical treatment will decrease the lamellar spacing.
The thermomechanical treatment will reorient and improve the alignment of the lamellar colonies.
Decreased lamellar spacing and improved colony alignment will create continuous dislocation-transmission paths.
Refining and reorienting the lamellar microstructure will reduce barriers to dislocation motion at internal boundaries.
Reduced boundary barriers will allow smoother dislocation transmission and mitigate dislocation pile-ups.
Mitigating dislocation pile-ups will reduce local stress concentrations and microcrack initiation.
The processed alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature tensile elongation than the untreated alloy.
The processed alloy will retain or slightly increase its yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The processed alloy will retain or slightly increase its ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The intervention is applicable to eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar morphologies under room-temperature tensile loading.
The effects may not transfer to substantially different microstructures or non-room-temperature conditions.
